questions.stem: A central network team owns all VPCs. Workload accounts must launch resources directly in shared subnets owned by the network account (not their own copy). Which fits?

options.text: AWS Resource Access Manager (RAM) — share VPC subnets from the network account to the workload accounts.
VPC peering between every account pair.
A Direct Connect to each workload account.
Manually copying subnet IDs into each account.

questions.explanation: RAM enables shared VPC subnets owned by the network account. Workload accounts launch ENIs directly in them. Peering doesn't share subnets.

questions.stem: A regulated company wants pre-built guardrails (preventive SCPs + detective Config rules), a log-archive + audit account, and Account Factory for new account vending. Which fits?

options.text: AWS Control Tower (with Account Factory and pre-built guardrails).

questions.explanation: Control Tower automates landing-zone creation with guardrails and Account Factory. The other options are off-pattern.

questions.stem: A central tooling account vends standardised, pre-approved CloudFormation products to engineering teams in member accounts (e.g., approved RDS configurations) with per-product IAM scoping. Which fits?

options.text: AWS Service Catalog (Portfolio + Product + cross-account sharing).

questions.explanation: Service Catalog is the AWS-native curated-product offering with cross-account sharing. The other options aren't product catalogs.

questions.stem: Multiple regions and accounts need centrally-managed global network policy, segmentation, and a unified dashboard — beyond what TGW alone offers. Which fits?

options.text: A NAT Gateway in every account.

questions.explanation: Cloud WAN is the AWS managed global WAN for multi-region/account network policy. The other options don't scale.

questions.stem: A security team needs to ensure that NEW resources created across an Organization always inherit a baseline (e.g., S3 Block Public Access, default encryption). Which combination fits?

options.text: Service Control Policies (preventive) + AWS Config Conformance Packs (detective + remediation) + Account Factory baseline (Control Tower).

questions.explanation: Layered preventive (SCP) + detective (Config) + provisioning baselines is the documented multi-account governance pattern.

questions.stem: You want CloudTrail organization trail centralised in one account, with logs encrypted by a customer-managed KMS key the audit team controls. Which configuration fits?

options.text: Organisation trail in the management account → audit account's S3 bucket; the bucket policy and KMS key policy explicitly grant CloudTrail and the audit team access.
A trail in each account, no central bucket.

questions.explanation: Org trail to a centrally-controlled audit bucket with KMS is the documented log-archive pattern. Per-account trails miss centralisation; the other options are off-pattern.

questions.stem: A workforce with Active Directory needs SSO into AWS accounts AND into 30 SaaS apps. Which fits?

options.text: AWS IAM Identity Center connected to AD (managed AD or AD Connector) — SSO into AWS accounts and SAML/OIDC SaaS apps with permission sets and app assignments.

questions.explanation: IAM Identity Center supports AD as identity source and SaaS-app SSO. The other options don't scale or are unsafe.

questions.stem: Which TWO are valid uses of AWS Organizations Service Control Policies (SCPs)?

options.text: Restrict member accounts to specific approved AWS regions.
Block specific high-risk APIs (e.g., `ec2:DisableImageDeprecation`) across all principals in target OU.
Grant permissions to users (SCPs are deny-only — they don't grant).
Apply outside the AWS Organization boundary.

questions.explanation: SCPs are guardrails (deny-only) targeting accounts/OUs. They don't grant or manage credentials, and only apply within an Organization.

questions.stem: Which TWO statements about AWS RAM are TRUE?

options.text: RAM can share VPC subnets, Transit Gateways, License Manager configs, Route 53 Resolver rules, and more across an Organization.
RAM allows the resource owner to retain operational control while consumers use the resource directly in their own account.
RAM transfers ownership of resources between accounts.
RAM is only for S3 buckets.
RAM cannot share with an entire Organization.

questions.explanation: A and B describe RAM accurately. RAM does NOT transfer ownership, supports many resource types beyond S3, and CAN share Organization-wide.

questions.stem: A global write-anywhere read-anywhere NoSQL workload needs ms latency from any region with active-active multi-region writes. Which fits?

options.text: Aurora Global Database (single primary writer; not active-active).

questions.explanation: Global Tables = active-active multi-region NoSQL. Aurora Global has one writer. Self-managed defeats managed-service goal.

questions.stem: A global object-storage workload needs a single S3 endpoint that auto-routes clients to the lowest-latency healthy bucket in multiple regions. Which fits?

options.text: S3 Multi-Region Access Points (MRAP) with failover routing.
Direct Connect to one region only.

questions.explanation: MRAP gives a single global endpoint with replicated buckets and intelligent routing/failover. The other options are inferior or wrong.

questions.stem: A workload requires sub-5-millisecond latency from end-user mobile devices on 5G — beyond regular regions. Which AWS option fits?

options.text: AWS Wavelength (5G edge inside carrier networks).

questions.explanation: Wavelength runs AWS compute inside 5G carrier networks for ultra-low-latency mobile workloads. The other options don't reach that latency floor.

questions.stem: A regulated workload requires AWS managed services running ON premises (e.g., for data-residency compliance). Which fits?

options.text: AWS Outposts (rack or server) — managed AWS services in your data center.
Snowball Edge for years at a time.

questions.explanation: Outposts is the AWS managed-on-prem hardware for data-residency / latency requirements. The other options aren't managed AWS on-prem.

questions.stem: A multi-region active-passive web app needs a single global static IP, fast failover, and TCP/UDP support — beyond what CloudFront offers. Which fits?
questions.explanation: Global Accelerator gives static anycast IPs + AWS-edge acceleration for TCP/UDP across regions, with health-aware failover. CloudFront is HTTP-only.

questions.stem: A multi-region encryption strategy requires the SAME KMS key (key material) usable in two regions for encrypting and decrypting cross-region replicated data. Which fits?

options.text: KMS multi-region keys (replica keys in multiple regions sharing the same key material and ID).

questions.explanation: Multi-region keys allow same key material in multiple regions. Single-region CMKs are not portable. AWS-owned keys aren't customer-controlled.

questions.stem: A workload has bursty intermittent traffic at unpredictable times. The DB tier should auto-scale capacity DOWN to near-zero when idle. Which fits?

options.text: Aurora Serverless v2 — auto-scales ACUs (capacity units) down to a low minimum.
Aurora Provisioned with the largest instance class always running.

questions.explanation: Aurora Serverless v2 is the scale-on-demand option ideal for bursty workloads. The other options always cost.

questions.stem: A long-running batch workflow (>5 minutes) with branches and retries that touches many AWS services. Which Step Functions workflow type fits?

options.text: Step Functions Standard (up to 1 year, full execution history, exactly-once).

questions.explanation: Standard supports long durations and full audit. Express is for short high-throughput. Long-running monoliths in Lambda hit the 15-min cap.

questions.stem: A workload uses ECS on EC2 today. The team wants to remove all instance management overhead while keeping ECS task definitions and integrations. Which fits?

options.text: Switch the task launch type to AWS Fargate (serverless container compute).
Switch to EC2 t2.micro for everything.
Migrate to Lambda regardless of fit.

questions.explanation: ECS Fargate keeps ECS abstractions while removing instance management. The other options don't match the requirement.

questions.stem: Which TWO are documented patterns for an event-driven, loosely-coupled architecture on AWS?

options.text: SNS topic with multiple SQS subscribers (fan-out).
EventBridge rules routing service events to Lambda or Step Functions.
Producers calling consumers synchronously over SSH for every event.
Storing all events in a SQLite file on a developer's laptop.
A static text file polled every second.

questions.explanation: SNS+SQS and EventBridge are the two canonical AWS pub/sub and event-routing primitives.

questions.stem: Which TWO statements about Direct Connect resilience are TRUE?

options.text: For high resilience, use multiple Direct Connect connections terminating at multiple Direct Connect locations across multiple devices.
Site-to-Site VPN can serve as encrypted backup for Direct Connect using BGP path preference.
A single Direct Connect connection without backup is sufficient for a "highly available" architecture.
Direct Connect cannot be combined with Site-to-Site VPN.
Direct Connect provides built-in encryption by default (it does not — MACsec is opt-in for selected port speeds).

questions.explanation: A and B are documented HA patterns. The other statements are wrong.

questions.stem: You discover EBS gp2 volumes attached to many instances. The team wants better performance and lower cost. Which migration is recommended?

options.text: Migrate to gp3 — independent IOPS/throughput provisioning, generally cheaper and more flexible than gp2.

questions.explanation: gp3 is generally cheaper and more flexible than gp2. Magnetic / HDD are slower; staying on gp2 forgoes savings.

questions.stem: A 50TB S3 bucket has unknown access patterns — some objects are hot, others cold, with high variability. Which storage class minimises cost without performance trade-offs?

options.text: S3 Intelligent-Tiering — automatically moves objects between tiers based on observed access patterns.
S3 Glacier Deep Archive (multi-hour retrieval — wrong for hot/cold mix).

questions.explanation: Intelligent-Tiering monitors and tiers automatically — ideal for unknown/changing patterns. Deep Archive breaks hot access.

questions.stem: A SaaS website is single-region in `us-east-1`. Read-heavy global users complain about latency. Which is the lowest-effort improvement?

options.text: Add CloudFront in front with appropriate cache TTLs.
Migrate to a different cloud provider.
Move the database to read-only on the client devices.

questions.explanation: CloudFront delivers cached content from edge globally — the canonical low-effort latency improvement.

questions.stem: You want continuous, multi-account visibility into right-sizing recommendations and Savings Plans / RI gaps. Which fits?
questions.explanation: Cost Explorer + Compute Optimizer with Organization access is the documented continuous-cost-optimisation pair.

questions.stem: A team uses RDS PostgreSQL with single-AZ. They want HA with no app code changes and < 60s failover. Which fits?

options.text: Enable Multi-AZ for RDS — synchronous standby with same DNS endpoint and automated failover.
A pair of unrelated DBs and copy nightly.

questions.explanation: Multi-AZ is the documented RDS HA primitive. Read replicas are not HA. The other options are not equivalent.

questions.stem: An existing workload uses a Classic Load Balancer (CLB). The team wants L7 features (path/host routing, gRPC, WebSocket). Which fits?

options.text: Replace LB with a single EC2.

questions.explanation: ALB is the modern L7 LB. NLB is L4. CLB is deprecated. Single EC2 isn't a load balancer.

questions.stem: Stakeholders want a structured Well-Architected review of an existing workload across the 6 pillars. Which fits?

options.text: AWS Well-Architected Tool review with appropriate lenses (Serverless, ML, etc.).

questions.explanation: WA Tool is the structured review tool. Trusted Advisor / Compute Optimizer are narrower.

questions.stem: Which TWO actions improve resilience of an existing single-AZ stateless web tier at lowest effort?

options.text: Move EC2 fleet behind an ALB across multiple AZs with an Auto Scaling group.
Use cross-zone load balancing on the ALB so traffic is balanced evenly across all healthy targets.
Run a single oversized EC2 instance.

questions.explanation: Multi-AZ ASG behind ALB + cross-zone LB are documented foundational resilience patterns.

questions.stem: Which TWO are documented cost-optimisation actions for steady-state EC2 baselines?

options.text: Right-size with Compute Optimizer recommendations BEFORE committing to Savings Plans.
Use Spot Instances for interruption-tolerant tiers.
Always buy 3-year No-Upfront RIs at current oversized capacity.
Use root credentials for CI to skip IAM cost.

questions.explanation: Right-size first, then commit; Spot for fault-tolerant. The other options waste money or are anti-patterns.

questions.stem: You want a single pane of glass to track multiple migrations, sources, and statuses across AWS Application Migration Service, DMS, and partner tools. Which fits?
questions.explanation: Migration Hub aggregates migration progress across tools. The other options aren't.

questions.stem: You're moving 100 TB of file shares from on-prem NAS to S3 over an existing 1 Gbps WAN. Which fits?

options.text: AWS DataSync — managed, parallelised, encrypted file/object transfer with bandwidth limits and incremental syncs.
Manual rsync from a single laptop.
Snowball Edge (offline) — faster only if the WAN is too slow; with 1 Gbps and 100 TB, online via DataSync is reasonable.

questions.explanation: DataSync is purpose-built for online migration of file/object data. Snowball is the offline alternative for low-bandwidth scenarios.

questions.stem: On-prem applications need ongoing access to AWS storage backed by S3 with NFS/SMB semantics for users. Which fits?

options.text: AWS Storage Gateway (File Gateway / Volume Gateway / Tape Gateway).
A 24/7 EC2 host with manual rsync.

questions.explanation: Storage Gateway is the bridge between on-prem and AWS storage with NFS/SMB/iSCSI/VTL semantics.

questions.stem: Migrating a heterogeneous database (Oracle → Aurora PostgreSQL) requires schema + code conversion plus continuous data replication. Which combination fits?

options.text: AWS SCT for schema/code conversion + AWS DMS for ongoing replication and final cutover.
A single mysqldump emailed to the DBA.

questions.explanation: SCT + DMS is the documented heterogeneous DB migration path. The others aren't.

questions.stem: A team wants to lift-and-shift a fleet of VMware VMs to EC2 with continuous block-level replication so cutover is fast and tested. Which fits?
questions.explanation: MGN is the AWS lift-and-shift tool with block-level continuous replication and orchestrated cutover.

questions.stem: Which TWO statements about modernization paths are TRUE?

options.text: Replatform from self-managed MySQL on EC2 to Aurora MySQL reduces operational overhead while keeping the engine.
Refactor a monolith to microservices on ECS / EKS / Lambda can improve scalability and deployment velocity, but is a longer effort.
Modernization always requires rewriting all code in one sprint.
Lift-and-shift workloads cannot benefit from Auto Scaling.
Managed services should be avoided because of vendor lock-in.

questions.explanation: A and B are correct. Modernization is iterative; lift-and-shift workloads still benefit from Auto Scaling; managed services usually win on TCO.
